stories.headline: U.S. Inflation Accelerates to 3.8% in April, Driven by Energy Costs From Iran War
stories.summary:
The Consumer Price Index rose 3.8% annually in April, exceeding the Dow Jones consensus forecast of 3.7% and marking the highest inflation reading since May 2023. Higher energy costs — stemming from the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict — have replaced tariffs as the primary driver of price increases for American consumers.

The surge in energy and petrochemical prices reflects the severe disruption to global supply chains caused by the military confrontation with Iran. Analysts warn that sustained closure of the Hormuz strait could keep upward pressure on prices well into the summer, complicating the Federal Reserve's policy calculus.

The inflation data lands as President Trump is in Beijing for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, where trade, tariffs, and the Iran war are all on the agenda. Trump has publicly dismissed Iranian counter-proposals to end the conflict as unacceptable, and U.S. officials say the military option remains under active consideration.

The report will intensify the political debate over the economic costs of the Iran war. Critics argue the administration has underestimated the inflationary fallout of prolonged military action in the Gulf, while supporters contend that a decisive resolution to Iran's nuclear program is worth the short-term economic pain.

stories.headline: Hamas 'Weaponised' Sexual Violence on Oct. 7, Comprehensive Israeli Investigation Concludes
stories.summary:
A 300-page independent Israeli investigation has concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups engaged in "systematic, widespread" sexual violence during the October 7, 2023, attacks, with rapes, sexual assault, and sexual torture deployed intentionally "to maximize pain and suffering." The report is the most comprehensive investigation to date, drawing on 430 filmed survivor and witness interviews, more than 10,000 photographs and videos filmed by attackers, and official forensic records.

The Civil Commission found recurring accounts of violent gang rape at the Nova music festival, genital mutilation of victims, and sexual violence against hostages held in Gaza over prolonged periods — affecting both men and women. Among the most harrowing findings, the report describes two young relatives being forced by captors to perform sex acts on each other, which investigators said reflected a deliberate pattern of exploiting family bonds as instruments of terror.

The report concludes the crimes "constitute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocidal acts under international law." Evidence has been preserved in a secure archive to support future prosecutions. Hamas has repeatedly denied that any sexual violence occurred during the attacks or against hostages.

While prior UN reports had found "reasonable grounds to believe" sexual violence had occurred, this investigation represents a significant escalation in the formal documentation of alleged atrocities. The findings are likely to intensify international legal proceedings and renewed calls for accountability, even as the broader Gaza conflict continues.

stories.headline: Macron Announces $27 Billion African Investment Package at Nairobi Summit in Pivot Away From Colonial-Era Ties
stories.summary:
French President Emmanuel Macron co-hosted the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, Kenya on Tuesday alongside Kenyan President William Ruto, announcing $27 billion in French investment across energy transition, digital infrastructure, AI, the maritime economy, and agriculture. The summit is the first of its kind held in an English-speaking African country, a deliberate symbolic departure from France's traditional practice of convening such meetings in Paris or Francophone Africa.

Macron repeatedly invoked the language of "co-investment" and "equal footing partnerships," and invited African business leaders to invest in France in return. The investment package is projected to create approximately 250,000 jobs across both Africa and France.

The summit comes against a backdrop of sharply rising anti-French sentiment across West Africa, where several former French colonies have expelled French troops and sought ties with Russia and China in recent years. French influence on the continent has been in accelerating decline, and analysts say the choice of Kenya signals Paris is attempting a structural reset — broadening engagement beyond its historically Francophone sphere.

Kenya's Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi framed the summit as a chance to dismantle "artificial" linguistic barriers and build deeper pan-African integration. Senegal-based analyst Gilles Yabi told the BBC that a new generation of Africans is demanding a definitive break from colonial and post-colonial influence, putting pressure on Macron to demonstrate that the rhetorical shift translates into substantive policy change.

stories.headline: Update: FDA Commissioner Marty Makary Resigns Amid Trump Dissatisfaction
stories.summary:
Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Marty Makary announced his resignation Tuesday after 13 months in the role, becoming the fourth high-profile Trump administration departure this year. Deputy Commissioner for Food Kyle Diamantas will serve as acting commissioner. President Trump, when asked about Makary, said: 'He's a great doctor and he was having some difficulty, but he's going to go on and he's going to do well.'

Makary's tenure was marked by significant turbulence, including mass layoffs, leadership upheaval, and a series of controversies in which the agency's scientific principles were perceived by critics as being overridden by political interests. The FDA operates under the broader health policy direction of Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose aggressive reform agenda generated repeated friction with career staff and outside stakeholders.

The FDA regulates approximately one-fifth of the U.S. economy, meaning leadership instability at the agency carries wide-ranging consequences for drug approvals, food safety, and the pharmaceutical and medical device industries. Supporters of the administration had argued Makary was pursuing necessary reforms to an entrenched bureaucracy; critics contended the turmoil undermined the agency's credibility and scientific independence.

The resignation was first reported by Politico Pro and quickly confirmed by multiple outlets. No timeline has been given for naming a permanent replacement.

stories.headline: CBO Estimates Trump's 'Golden Dome' Missile Defense System Would Cost $1.2 Trillion
stories.summary:
A new analysis from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimates that President Trump's proposed 'Golden Dome' space-based missile defense system would cost approximately $1.2 trillion over 20 years — nearly seven times the $175 billion price tag Trump cited when announcing the program last year. The CBO cautioned its analysis reflects 'one illustrative approach rather than an estimate of a specific Administration proposal,' citing a lack of detailed specifications from the Defense Department.

Trump ordered the Golden Dome program by executive order during his first week in office and pledged it would be 'fully operational' before his term ends in January 2029. The system is envisioned to include ground- and space-based capabilities to detect, intercept, and destroy incoming missiles at all stages of flight, partly modeled on Israel's layered air defense architecture. Congress has already appropriated roughly $24 billion for the initiative.

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), who requested the CBO estimate, said the program was 'nothing more than a massive giveaway to defense contractors paid for entirely by working Americans.' Supporters of the program argue the escalating threat from peer adversaries — including advanced hypersonic and intercontinental ballistic missiles developed by China and Russia — justifies the investment regardless of cost.

The CBO's previous estimate had already placed the space-based components alone at up to $542 billion over 20 years, suggesting the full-system figure has been widely understood in budget circles to far exceed the White House's initial public estimate.

stories.headline: Zelensky's Former Chief of Staff Appears in Court as Ukraine Corruption Probe Escalates
stories.summary:
Andriy Yermak, until recently President Volodymyr Zelensky's closest adviser and chief of staff, appeared in a Kyiv court Tuesday after Ukraine's two anti-corruption agencies named him a suspect in a money-laundering scheme tied to a $10.5 million luxury construction project outside the capital. Prosecutors asked the court to either detain Yermak or set bail of approximately $4 million. Yermak told reporters he owns only 'one flat and one car' and denied wrongdoing; his lawyer called the allegations 'baseless.'

The case is part of the broader 'Operation Midas,' a sweeping anti-corruption investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme in Ukraine's nuclear energy sector. Former Deputy Prime Minister Oleksiy Chernyshov has been charged with abuse of office, ex-Energy Minister Herman Haluschenko was detained attempting to leave the country, and businessman Timur Mindich — once part of Zelensky's inner circle — reportedly fled to Israel. Anti-corruption officials stressed Zelensky himself is not a subject of the investigation.

Yermak led Ukraine's negotiations with the United States throughout Russia's full-scale invasion and was considered the second-most powerful figure in the Ukrainian government until his resignation last November following a raid on his apartment. The corruption allegations have complicated Ukraine's EU accession bid; last year Zelensky was forced to rescind a law seen as weakening the independence of the anti-corruption agencies after protests and EU pressure.

The case carries significant geopolitical weight at a moment when Ukraine is heavily dependent on Western financial and military support. Continued high-profile corruption findings could complicate ongoing aid discussions and reinforce concerns among some Western lawmakers about accountability for funds sent to Kyiv.

stories.headline: Putin Announces Deployment of Nuclear-Capable Sarmat ICBM by Year's End
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin declared Tuesday that Russia will deploy its Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missile — capable of carrying multiple nuclear warheads — by the end of 2026, following what Moscow described as a successful test of the weapon. The announcement came as Russia and Ukraine resumed strikes against one another following the expiration of a short-term ceasefire, and months after the last remaining U.S.-Russia nuclear arms control treaty, New START, expired without renewal.

The Sarmat, known in NATO parlance as the SS-X-30 'Satan II,' is designed to evade missile defense systems and can reportedly carry up to 15 independently targeted nuclear warheads. Russia had announced the missile's development years ago but its operational deployment has faced repeated delays. Putin's statement signals Moscow's intent to modernize its nuclear arsenal even as diplomatic channels with Washington remain strained.

The timing of the announcement — coinciding with the breakdown of the U.S.-brokered ceasefire in Ukraine — was widely seen as a deliberate strategic signal. No immediate response from the White House or NATO was issued Tuesday. Arms control analysts have warned that the expiration of New START has left no formal verification mechanism in place for either side to monitor the other's strategic nuclear forces.

The Sarmat deployment pledge adds a new dimension to already elevated nuclear tensions between Moscow and Western capitals. It comes as President Trump is simultaneously engaged in high-stakes diplomatic summitry with China in Beijing, where nuclear and strategic stability issues are also on the agenda.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Xi Beijing Summit Opens as U.S. Presses China on Iran, Trade, and Fertilizer Hoarding
stories.summary:
U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in Beijing for a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, with preparations including heightened security around Tiananmen Square and an itinerary featuring formal talks, a state banquet, and a visit to the Temple of Heaven. The summit is being described by analysts as one of the most consequential U.S.-China encounters in years, with the future of global trade, Taiwan tensions, and competition in advanced technology all on the agenda.

A central focus is the ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has severely disrupted global oil and fertilizer shipments. China has been quietly positioning itself as a mediator alongside Pakistan, presenting a five-point ceasefire plan and nudging Iranian officials toward negotiations. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said publicly he hoped China would tell Iran's foreign minister, who visited Beijing last week, that blocking the Strait was causing global isolation.

Separately, former World Bank President David Malpass called on China to stop hoarding food and fertilizer stockpiles, warning that global supply disruptions are costing billions of meals per week and hitting the poorest countries hardest. China halted fertilizer exports in March, citing domestic needs; a Chinese embassy spokesperson rejected the criticism, saying the root causes of supply disruptions could not be shifted onto Beijing.

The summit carries enormous economic weight for both sides. China's economy is under strain from slower growth, higher unemployment, and rising petrochemical costs tied to the Iran conflict, giving Xi incentive to help broker a resolution — but also leverage to extract concessions from Washington. Analysts say the outcomes of this meeting could shape U.S.-China relations and global stability for years.

stories.headline: Criminal Charges Filed Against Dali Ship Operator Over Deadly Baltimore Bridge Collapse
stories.summary:
Federal prosecutors unsealed a criminal indictment Tuesday against Synergy Marine, the Singapore- and India-based operator of the cargo ship Dali, and one of its employees over the March 2024 collapse of Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge, which killed six construction workers. Synergy and its technical supervisor Radhakrishnan Karthik Nair face charges including conspiracy, obstruction, and misconduct resulting in death.

Prosecutors allege the Dali lost power twice in a four-minute span before striking the bridge, with the first outage caused by a loose wire in a switchboard and the second caused by an improperly used flushing pump supplying fuel to generators — a configuration the vessel was not approved to use. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche called the collapse "a preventable tragedy of enormous consequence" and said the indictment was a critical step toward accountability for what he described as reckless disregard for maritime safety regulations.

According to the indictment, Synergy employees knew about the improper pump use and "took steps to hide" it on the Dali and other vessels, and the company also allegedly falsified safety records. Synergy said it "will defend against these allegations with vigor." The company has already paid more than $100 million to the Justice Department in a civil settlement and $350 million to Maryland's insurer, and faces another civil trial next month.

The charges mark the first criminal accountability action in one of the most economically disruptive infrastructure disasters in recent U.S. history. Baltimore is still working to reconstruct the bridge, a project expected to take years and cost billions of dollars.

stories.headline: McConnell Breaks With Hegseth Over Pentagon Budget, Warns of Alienating Allies
stories.summary:
Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee Chairman Mitch McConnell pressed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Tuesday over the Trump administration's $1.5 trillion fiscal year 2027 Pentagon budget request, raising pointed objections about how key programs — including the Golden Dome missile defense initiative — would be funded. McConnell also rebuked Hegseth for what he characterized as alienating U.S. allies at a moment of multiple major world conflicts, including the ongoing war with Iran.

The public clash between the Senate's senior Republican and the Trump administration's Defense Secretary underscores growing intraparty friction over defense spending priorities and alliance management. McConnell has historically been among the most hawkish voices in the GOP on defense funding and U.S. alliance commitments, placing him at odds with elements of the Trump administration's approach.

The hearing comes as Pentagon officials make their case on Capitol Hill for one of the largest defense budget requests in U.S. history, framed in part around the demands of the Iran conflict now in its third month. The budget debate will shape military readiness and alliance relationships at a critical juncture in U.S. foreign policy.

stories.headline: Update: UN Confirms 269 Killed in Pakistani Airstrike on Afghan Drug Rehab Centre, War Crime Probe Sought
stories.summary:
A United Nations report released Tuesday confirmed at least 269 people were killed in a Pakistani airstrike on the Omid Drug Rehabilitation Hospital in Kabul — the deadliest single attack in Afghanistan's modern history, surpassing casualty figures from two decades of NATO-era combat. The UN was granted access to the site and confirmed the strike hit civilians undergoing treatment for drug addiction. Human Rights Watch has called the attack "an unlawful attack and a possible war crime."

Pakistan disputes that it struck a civilian facility, stating in a response to the BBC that "no hospital, no drug rehabilitation centre, and no civilian facility was targeted" and that the strike was aimed at "military and terrorist infrastructure." The site, Camp Phoenix, is a former U.S. and NATO military compound that was converted into a rehabilitation centre in 2016, five years before the Taliban returned to power. Islamabad has long accused the Taliban government of sheltering militants responsible for attacks inside Pakistan; Kabul denies the charge.

Families of more than 30 confirmed victims — including recovering addicts and hospital staff — reject Pakistan's account. Many bodies were so badly burned or fragmented that identification was impossible, with some relatives locating loved ones only by birthmarks or partial remains. The UN acknowledged the true death toll is likely significantly higher than the 269 confirmed figure.

The strike marks a sharp escalation in months of cross-border fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan. Calls are growing for an independent international investigation into whether the attack constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law, though no formal tribunal has been announced.

stories.headline: Philippine Senator Flees ICC Arrest, Takes Refuge in Senate as Duterte Dynasty Feud Deepens
stories.summary:
Philippine Senator Ronald Dela Rosa, the former national police chief who oversaw Rodrigo Duterte's deadly war on drugs, escaped arrest Tuesday after the International Criminal Court unsealed a warrant charging him as an indirect co-perpetrator in the killings of at least 32 people between 2016 and 2018. Security footage showed National Bureau of Investigation agents chasing Dela Rosa through Senate corridors before he reached the chamber and was placed under its protective custody. Police subsequently announced they would not arrest him while he remained inside the Senate.

The ICC warrant follows the March 2025 arrest of former President Duterte himself, who is currently in custody in The Hague. Dela Rosa has vowed to remain within the Senate building and has asked the Philippine Supreme Court to block his arrest on the grounds that no valid local judicial warrant exists. The Philippine Senate, dominated by Duterte allies, elected a new president Monday who declared the chamber would only act on warrants issued by Philippine courts.

The standoff deepens a bitter feud between the Duterte and Marcos political dynasties. Earlier the same day, the Marcos-aligned House of Representatives voted to impeach Vice President Sara Duterte — Rodrigo Duterte's daughter — for the second time. Sara Duterte, who is a leading contender in the 2028 presidential race, has accused President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of weaponizing the ICC process and impeachment proceedings to neutralize her political future.

The crisis raises fundamental questions about the Philippines' obligations under international law. The elder Duterte has argued that the ICC has no jurisdiction because Manila withdrew from the Rome Statute in 2019, but ICC judges rejected that argument last month, ruling that the alleged crimes occurred before the withdrawal took effect.

stories.headline: eBay Rejects GameStop's $55.5 Billion Takeover Bid as 'Neither Credible Nor Attractive'
stories.summary:
EBay's board of directors formally rejected an unsolicited $55.5 billion takeover offer from GameStop on Tuesday, with board chairman Paul Pressler calling the proposal "neither credible nor attractive." GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen had offered $125 per share in a mix of cash and stock, contingent on securing outside equity and debt financing — a structure that Wall Street analysts had already greeted with deep skepticism given that GameStop's own market capitalization stands at roughly $10.4 billion compared to eBay's $47.8 billion.

Pressler's rejection letter cited concerns over the uncertainty of GameStop's financing, the operational and leverage risks of combining the two companies, the impact on eBay's long-term growth, and questions about GameStop's governance and executive incentives. EBay said it remains confident in its standalone strategy, pointing to its focused marketplace, improved seller experience, and consistent shareholder returns.

Cohen had argued the combination would give eBay access to GameStop's approximately 1,600 U.S. retail stores for authentication, intake, fulfillment, and live commerce operations, with Cohen serving as CEO of the merged entity. He has indicated he may pursue a hostile bid by taking the proposal directly to eBay shareholders — a tactic similar to the one Paramount Skydance's David Ellison threatened before ultimately acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery.

The episode underscores the ongoing transformation efforts at GameStop, which has struggled to adapt its brick-and-mortar retail model to a digital gaming landscape. Cohen's aggressive dealmaking has kept the company in headlines but has yet to produce a transformative transaction.

stories.headline: New Treatments Offer Breakthrough Hope for Pancreatic Cancer Patients
stories.summary:
Pancreatic cancer, long one of the most lethal malignancies with a five-year survival rate below 12 percent, is showing signs of becoming more treatable as a new generation of therapies moves through clinical development. Among the most promising is daraxonrasib, a drug targeting the KRAS gene mutation present in roughly 90 percent of pancreatic tumors, alongside advances in mRNA-based personalized vaccines that teach the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells.

Researchers report that the new KRAS-targeting strategy also holds potential for lung and colon cancers, which share similar mutation profiles, significantly broadening the implications of the research beyond pancreatic disease alone. Early trial results have been described as encouraging, with some patients achieving measurable tumor reduction where previous treatments had failed entirely.

The developments are generating cautious optimism among oncologists, who caution that pancreatic cancer is typically diagnosed at a late stage when it has already spread, limiting the effectiveness of even novel therapies. Larger clinical trials are needed to confirm the results seen in early-phase studies before these treatments become standard of care.

The progress reflects a broader acceleration in cancer research driven by advances in genomic sequencing and mRNA technology, the same platform underlying COVID-19 vaccines. Scientists say the pancreatic cancer breakthroughs illustrate how understanding the molecular drivers of tumors is enabling more targeted, potentially more effective interventions.

stories.headline: Update: Israel Passes Death Penalty Law for Oct. 7 Attackers as Iran Rejects U.S. Ceasefire Terms
stories.summary:
Israel's parliament passed legislation Monday permitting the death penalty and public military tribunals for those involved in the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attacks. The move, long debated within Israeli society, marks a significant escalation in how the country intends to prosecute suspects linked to the assault that killed approximately 1,200 people and took roughly 250 hostage.

On the diplomatic front, President Trump publicly rejected Iran's counteroffer to end the Gulf war, calling the month-long ceasefire 'unbelievably weak' and describing it as on 'massive life support.' Iran's conditions reportedly include lifting of the U.S. naval blockade, recognition of Iranian sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, and compensation for war damage — terms the Trump administration has dismissed as non-starters.

The rejection deepens uncertainty over the fragile ceasefire. With the Strait of Hormuz dispute unresolved, global fertilizer and food supply chains remain under severe strain, and J.P. Morgan has forecast oil prices above $100 for the rest of 2026. Meanwhile, Iran-backed Hezbollah and Israel continued to exchange fire in Lebanon despite a separate U.S.-brokered ceasefire announced last month.

Supporters of the Israeli death penalty law argue it delivers proportionate justice for unprecedented atrocities; critics, including some Israeli legal experts and human rights groups, warn it risks undermining rule-of-law norms and could complicate hostage negotiations. The dual crises — Israel's domestic legal moves and the stalled Iran talks — leave the broader Middle East situation deeply volatile.

stories.headline: Update: French Hantavirus Patient Critical After Misdiagnosis; Dutch Hospital Workers Quarantined
stories.summary:
A French woman who disembarked from the hantavirus-stricken cruise ship MV Hondius is in critical condition in Paris after doctors initially dismissed her symptoms as anxiety or stress rather than viral infection. Spanish Health Minister Javier Padilla Bernáldez confirmed her flu-like symptoms had appeared to resolve before her condition deteriorated rapidly following her departure from the Canary Islands on Sunday. She was evacuated by air to a Paris hospital, where she is being treated by a specialized infectious disease unit.

Separately, 12 hospital workers at Radboudumc hospital in Nijmegen, Netherlands, were placed in a six-week precautionary quarantine after handling blood and urine samples from a hantavirus patient without adhering to strict PPE protocols. The development raises concerns about secondary exposure risks in healthcare settings.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Tuesday there is 'no sign' of a larger outbreak beginning, but cautioned that the virus's long incubation period means additional cases could still emerge in coming weeks. Seven cases have been confirmed overall, with three deaths. The MV Hondius, now evacuated of all passengers, is sailing to Rotterdam for sanitation.

Eighteen Americans previously repatriated remain under quarantine in the United States, with one passenger who tested weakly positive held in a Nebraska biocontainment unit. The Andes strain of hantavirus involved is notable for its capacity for human-to-human transmission, distinguishing it from most other hantavirus varieties.

stories.headline: California Mayor Resigns, Agrees to Plead Guilty to Acting as Covert Chinese Foreign Agent
stories.summary:
Eileen Wang, 58, the mayor of Arcadia, California, resigned abruptly Monday after the U.S. Department of Justice announced she had been charged with acting as an illegal covert foreign agent of China. Wang agreed to plead guilty to the felony count and faces up to 10 years in prison. Prosecutors allege she promoted pro-China propaganda and advanced the interests of Chinese officials while holding elected office.

Arcadia is a wealthy suburb of Los Angeles with a large Chinese-American population and has long been a focus of federal investigators examining Chinese political influence operations in Southern California. The case is part of a broader DOJ effort to identify and prosecute individuals operating on behalf of foreign governments without proper registration under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

The case highlights ongoing U.S. government concerns about Chinese government efforts to cultivate influence through local and state-level political figures, a strategy analysts say is difficult to detect and prosecute. The guilty plea, once formally entered, would make Wang one of the most senior elected U.S. officials to be convicted of acting as a foreign agent.

China's embassy in Washington did not immediately issue a public comment on the charges. The DOJ announcement comes amid already heightened U.S.-China tensions, with President Trump currently in Beijing for a summit with President Xi Jinping.

stories.headline: Canvas Maker Pays Ransom to Hackers Who Stole Data from 9,000 Universities
stories.summary:
Instructure, the company behind the widely used Canvas learning management system, has paid a ransom to the criminal hacking group Shiny Hunters after the group stole 3.5 terabytes of student and institutional data in a cyberattack that disrupted approximately 9,000 colleges and universities across the United States, Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom. The breach, discovered April 29, knocked Canvas offline for a period and disrupted online exams for tens of thousands of students.

Instructure confirmed it reached an 'agreement' with the hackers, who have stated they deleted the stolen data and will not extort students or institutions individually. The company framed the payment as a protective measure for students' data, though it did not disclose the financial terms. Cybersecurity experts and law enforcement agencies worldwide generally advise against paying ransoms, noting that criminals frequently keep stolen data for resale even after accepting payment — a pattern documented in the dismantling of the LockBit ransomware group.

The Shiny Hunters group, described as prolific in extortion operations, claimed the attack publicly online. Students sitting exams in the U.S. were among those most acutely affected; one meteorology student at Mississippi State University described a ransom message appearing mid-exam on their screen. The scale of the disruption — affecting nearly every major English-speaking country's higher education sector simultaneously — underscores the systemic vulnerability of centralized educational technology platforms.

Instructure said its priority was protecting students and education staff and noted it had maintained transparency with regular public updates throughout the incident, an unusual stance for a ransomware victim. The FBI and other law enforcement agencies were not named as having been consulted in Instructure's decision to pay.
